A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReVision research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched despite the changed title, terminology and organization.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation experiments, MTurk preference studies, TikTok dance-generation scores and comparisons between generation stages.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds VBench++, DAVIS, HumanML3D and KIT-ML results, alongside new user studies and ablations.

M1.justification: The three-stage pipeline, conditioning channels and perturbation-based prior training remain; PPPM is renamed PMP. v2 adds a long-video inference extension using motion interpolation/extrapolation and overlapping 32-frame clips with blended boundaries (Section 5.1), which v1 left to future work. Newly stated MSE supervision does not establish a changed training objective.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained Panda-70M subset, daily-activity evaluations and TikTok dances, v2 evaluates general video generation on VBench++, motion transfer on DAVIS, and standalone human-motion refinement on HumanML3D and KIT-ML. It also demonstrates 128-frame generation. These substantially broaden the evaluated data and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds comparisons with video generators including Wan2.1, DynamiCrafter, Step-Video-TI2V, Gen-4-I2V and Magi-1; DAVIS comparators MotionClone, ImageConductor and Go-with-the-Flow; and motion-generation comparators MotionDiffuse, ReMoDiffuse and MoMask. Disco is removed from the dance-results table, although its dataset split remains in use. The original SVD and HunyuanVideo preference comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 introduces Wan2.1 backbone evaluation, VBench++ metrics, DAVIS motion-transfer metrics and Top-1/2/3 R-Precision evaluation. Its efficiency experiment reduces Stage 1 resolution to one quarter, frames from 16 to 8, and denoising steps from 50 to 32. New occlusion ratings exclude responses without interactions. The former Stage 1/Stage 3 comparison is described as without/with PMP, without establishing whether the control or experiments actually changed.

E4.justification: v2 adds an efficiency-versus-quality preference study (Table 8), sensitivity to three confidence encodings (Table 9), prompt and motion-strength examples (Figure 11), and an occlusion case study and targeted preference evaluation (Figure 6, Table 4). The original mesh analysis is retained in Appendix C. The relabeled PMP study retains the earlier stage-comparison scores and is not additional numerical evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report seed 42 for the main paired-generation study and three raters per pair. v2 adds studies using descriptive scores and preference percentages but introduces no repeated-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests.

E6.justification: The full-motion TikTok row changes from SSIM 0.842 and FVD 137.53 in v1 Table 2 to 0.864 and 121.26 in v2 Table 5; target-pose FVD remains 130.14, and image-only FVD 136.43 is added. New benchmark and ablation tables substantially expand reported findings. Runtime changes from 77 to 49 seconds under reduced Stage 1 settings, rather than an unchanged evaluation configuration.

T1.justification: The diffusion equations, parametric-mesh definitions and 21-point general-object representation are retained, with some mathematics reformatted or relocated. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 adds no substantive formal derivation.

C1.justification: The title, abstract and contribution bullets replace explicit physics and physical-knowledge framing with parameterized model knowledge and object-centric motion knowledge. This modestly narrows the contribution's characterization. The central three-stage refinement claim, complex-motion benefits and headline comparison between 1.5B- and 13B-parameter models remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of Stage 1's scene and camera priors, depth-based occlusion handling, motion conditioning versus textual guidance, and confidence values as condition indicators. It also interprets PMP as a general motion denoiser. Existing limitations largely move unchanged to Appendix D, leaving its long-video future-work statement unreconciled with Section 5.1's new demonstration.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies shared PMP training across categories, pose-MSE supervision, the annotated dataset's approximately 55% human/15% animal/30% general-object composition, and absence of target poses in the original preference study. It also documents long-video window stride, overlap and blending. These are useful additions to documentation; the existing annotation pipeline and project-access information remain.

R1.justification: v2 substantially extends positioning into direct motion generation, motion-transfer systems and newer video backbones, citing and discussing methods such as MoMask, MotionDiffuse, Go-with-the-Flow and Wan2.1. Section 4.2 newly contrasts direct motion models' scene and camera limitations with motion extracted from video generators. The original related-work discussion is largely retained.

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes the manuscript by moving detailed dataset construction, the mesh analysis and limitations into Appendices B–D, and restructuring the main experimental narrative around PMP. Stage 1 receives substantial explanatory expansion. The title and PPPM/PMP terminology change throughout, and the appendix gains a broader-impact section.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column journal format. Figure 4 adds paired SVD comparisons; the stage visualization is rearranged into without/with-PMP pairs; and new benchmark tables, occlusion examples, long-video examples and conditioning visualizations are introduced. Existing mesh and architecture figures are retained and relocated or renumbered.

improvement.justification: v1's broad applicability claims rested mainly on SVD preference studies and a dance benchmark. v2 substantially strengthens their support through evaluation with another backbone, general-video and motion-transfer benchmarks, standalone motion refinement, and targeted efficiency and sensitivity tests. Added training details also improve assessability. These gains outweigh the unresolved relabeling of the stage comparison as a PMP ablation and the appendix's inconsistent long-video limitation.
